finding: Round 2 changed §4.2 so a success clears last_failure only when "(unit_kind, unit_id)" matches, justified by "id alone collides, since both record kinds are identified by a round number". §3.1 still ends with "Ids are unique within a run and are what `last_failure` clears on." Both halves of that sentence are now contradicted by the section that was repaired: ids are NOT unique within a run (a run doing review round 2 and audit round 2 has two units with id 2), and clearing is on the pair, not the id. Test 20 follows §4.2, so §3.1 is the stale copy.
suggestion: Rewrite §3.1's last sentence as: "A unit's id is unique within its kind, so `(kind, id)` identifies a unit — which is the key `last_failure` clears on (§4.2)."

finding: The only test seam the spec provides cannot exercise two of its own tests. `TP_RUNNER` is defined as "a runner object whose `args` are `["{unit_kind}", "{unit_id}", "{log_path}"]`" — it declares no `spend_key` and its arg template contains no `{max_budget_usd}` placeholder. Test 11 ("Spend is read from the runner's final log line") can therefore only ever exercise its negative half (spend null / cap-budget inert), and test 3 ("Each cap produces its own `stop_reason`") cannot produce `cap-budget` at all, because a run driven by the seam accrues no spend. The same gap makes §3.2's "`run_max_unit_budget_usd` of 0 omits the budget flag entirely rather than passing a literal 0" unobservable: the seam's template has no budget flag to omit or emit.
suggestion: Give the `TP_RUNNER` object a `spend_key` (e.g. `total_cost_usd`) and a `{max_budget_usd}` placeholder appended on the same condition as the `claude` template, and state that the fake runner writes a final JSON line carrying that key — so spend accrual, `cap-budget` and the flag-omission rule are all reachable from the seam.

finding: Three of the eight durable-write predicates are stated as changes with no baseline and no observation point, so no deterministic pass/fail test can be written and the Stop hook and the driver can legitimately disagree. `review-resolve` is "The spec's hash changed" — changed since when? Since the driver spawned the unit, since the run started, or since the last recorded round? `audit-fix` is "`HEAD` advanced" — advanced relative to which captured SHA, and does an unrelated concurrent commit satisfy it? `decompose` is "The task file holds at least one task" and `review-record`/`audit-record` are "A round file for round N exists": both are satisfied by state a *previous* unit left behind, so a unit that did nothing passes its own success test. §6.2 makes this worse by giving the same undefined column to the Stop hook, which has no access to the driver's pre-spawn snapshot unless the spec says one is exported.
suggestion: State that the driver captures each predicate's baseline immediately before spawning the unit and that the predicate is "differs from that baseline", and pass the baseline the Stop hook needs through the environment (as §3.1 already does for the other unit facts) — e.g. `TP_UNIT_BASELINE` carrying the spec hash / HEAD SHA / round number. For `decompose` and the record kinds, name a monotone condition (task count above the baseline; round file for a round number strictly greater than the baseline round).

finding: §3.3 asserts the durable-write column is read identically by the Stop hook (§6.2) and by the driver's own success test, but three of the eight conditions are not observable from inside the child. `audit-fix`'s 'HEAD advanced' and `review-resolve`'s 'the spec's hash changed' are deltas that need a pre-unit baseline, and the hook (which §6.2 forbids from reading `.tp/run.json`) has no place to get one. `decompose`'s 'the task file holds at least one task' is worse: after the first successful decompose it is already true, so on any later run the predicate passes before the unit does anything and both the hook and the driver score a no-op unit as a success.
suggestion: Give each delta predicate an explicit baseline the child can read — e.g. export `TP_UNIT_BASELINE` (HEAD sha, spec hash, task count) alongside the other unit variables in §3.1 — and restate `decompose`'s condition as a change relative to that baseline rather than as an absolute property of the task file.

finding: A retried unit reuses every artifact path of its failed attempt. §3.5's log path is `.tp/runs/<run-id>/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl` and §3.3/§6.3's role output is `$TP_RUN_DIR/$TP_UNIT_SEQ-$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson` — neither carries `attempt`, though `.tp/run.json` rows do. Two consequences the spec never resolves: attempt 2's log overwrites (or appends to) attempt 1's, so the spend key read from "the final line" may be the wrong run's; and a `review-role`/`audit-role` unit that crashed *after* writing a partial findings file leaves the durable-write predicate ("the file exists") already satisfied, so both the Stop hook and the driver's success test pass attempt 2 trivially — and attempt 1's truncated findings get merged into the round.
suggestion: Put `attempt` in the log path and in the role findings path (or have the driver delete the unit's artifacts before each retry), and say explicitly which attempt's file the record unit merges and which the spend key is read from.

finding: Round 2 replaced the stop hook's "run marker in `.tp/run.json`" with "predicates are observable, not inferences: … the durable write is the condition that kind names in §3.3's fourth column", and added "It never reads `.tp/run.json`." Three of the eight predicates §3.3 now supplies are relative, not observable: `review-resolve` = "The spec's hash changed", `audit-fix` = "`HEAD` advanced", `review-record`/`audit-record` = "A round file for round N exists". Changed and advanced against what baseline, and which N? The hook has TP_RUN_ID/TP_UNIT_* and the filesystem, and is explicitly denied the one file that records the pre-unit state. The repair removed the hook's only baseline source without giving the three relative predicates another one.
suggestion: Make each predicate absolute for the hook, or hand it a baseline through the environment. E.g. spawn the child with `TP_UNIT_BASELINE` (the pre-unit spec hash / HEAD sha / next round number) alongside the other TP_UNIT_* variables in §3.1, and restate §3.3's column in terms of it.

finding: Three of §3.3's durable-write predicates are deltas, not states, and §6.2 gives the Stop hook no baseline to compare against: `audit-fix` = "`HEAD` advanced" (advanced from which commit?), `review-resolve` = "The spec's hash changed" (changed from which hash?), and `decompose` = "The task file holds at least one task" (true before the unit starts whenever the file is non-empty). §6.2 explicitly forbids the hook from reading `.tp/run.json` and names only `TP_UNIT_KIND`, `TP_RUN_DIR` and `TP_UNIT_SEQ` as its inputs, so the implementer has to invent where the pre-unit HEAD/spec-hash is recorded and who writes it. The driver's own success test (§3.3: "both read the same condition") has the same hole.
suggestion: State that the driver records a per-unit baseline (HEAD sha, spec hash, task count) at spawn time in a per-unit file under `$TP_RUN_DIR` — e.g. `$TP_UNIT_SEQ-baseline.json` — and that the Stop hook and the driver both read it; or restate the three predicates as absolute conditions the hook can evaluate from env alone.

finding: "the `review-record` and `audit-record` units merge `$TP_RUN_DIR/*.ndjson` for the round" is not implementable as written: `TP_RUN_DIR` is per *run*, not per round (§3.5 shows one directory per `run-id`), while a run executes many review and audit rounds. Round 2's record unit globbing `$TP_RUN_DIR/*.ndjson` matches round 1's role files as well as its own, so every round after the first merges a superset — inflating the recorded finding count and the convergence arithmetic. The only distinguishing token in the filename is `$TP_UNIT_SEQ`, and nothing tells the record unit which seq range belongs to its round.
suggestion: Scope the findings path by round — e.g. `$TP_RUN_DIR/round-<N>/$TP_UNIT_SEQ-$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson`, or a `$TP_ROUND` variable in the child env — and state that the record unit merges only its own round's directory.

finding: The findings path is run-scoped but the merge is round-scoped. §3.5 makes the run directory per-run (`.tp/runs/<run-id>/`), §6.3 places every role file at `$TP_RUN_DIR/$TP_UNIT_SEQ-$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson` and has the record unit merge `$TP_RUN_DIR/*.ndjson` 'for the round'. A single run executes several review rounds (§3.1 loops until converged, §3.4 caps by units not rounds), so round 2's `review-record` unit would glob round 1's role files as well and record a round containing stale findings. The existing emitter already avoids this by putting the round in the filename (`review-r<N>-<role>.ndjson`); the spec's replacement drops the round and keeps the round-scoped merge claim.
suggestion: Scope the path or the glob to the round: either `$TP_RUN_DIR/r<round>/$TP_UNIT_SEQ-$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson` with the record unit merging that subdirectory, or keep the round in the basename and state the glob the record unit uses. Whichever is chosen, say explicitly which files a round-N record unit is allowed to merge.

finding: The round-2 findings-path repair made the role output `$TP_RUN_DIR/$TP_UNIT_SEQ-$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson` and the record units merge `$TP_RUN_DIR/*.ndjson` "for the round". But TP_RUN_DIR is run-scoped (§3.5's `.tp/runs/<run-id>/`), not round- or phase-scoped, while a single run is expected to execute several review rounds and then an audit phase (§3.1 loops, §3.4 caps). Round 2's `review-record` glob therefore also matches round 1's role files, and `audit-record`'s glob also matches every review role file in the same run. The old wording named per-file paths and never claimed a glob, so this collision is new in round 2.
suggestion: Scope the merge input, not the run: either write role files to `$TP_RUN_DIR/<phase>-<round>/$TP_UNIT_SEQ-$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson` and glob that subdirectory, or state that the record unit merges only the files whose `seq` belongs to its own iteration and name where it learns that set without reading `.tp/run.json` (§6.2 forbids that).

finding: §7 is entirely unpinned by §10. Seven new fields with explicit defaults and ranges (`run_max_units` 1-10000, `run_max_wall_clock_seconds` 60-604800, `run_max_budget_usd` 0-10000, `run_max_unit_budget_usd` 0-1000, `run_max_unit_retries` 0-5, `runner`, `notify_cmd`), the statement that they resolve through CLI > env > task override > project config > built-in, the carve-out that `notify_cmd` is read from `.tp/local.json` only, the claim that `tp config --resolved`, `tp config --extract` and `tp validate --project` cover them, and the `--compact` rule ("`stop_reason` and the cap totals survive; per-unit rows and log paths are stripped") have no test in 10.1-10.6. v0.31.1 shipped precisely because a repo-config field was missing from `--extract`/`validate --project`, and the fix was made durable with a config-assertion guard test; this spec re-creates that surface with no such test.
suggestion: Add a §10.2 test asserting each new field's default and both range boundaries (accepted at the endpoints, rejected one step outside), that a task-file override loses to a CLI flag and wins over project config, that `notify_cmd` set in `.tp/config.json` does NOT resolve while the same value in `.tp/local.json` does, that all seven appear in `tp config --resolved`/`--extract` and are validated by `tp validate --project`, and one `--compact` assertion naming the surviving and stripped keys.

finding: Test 5 — "Role units run concurrently and every other kind does not overlap them" — names no observable, so two engineers write different and differently-flaky assertions: one asserts overlapping wall-clock windows recorded by the fake runner (timing-dependent, and passes trivially on a fast machine only by luck), another asserts spawn order or process count, a third has the fake runner block on a rendezvous file. §3.2 defines what the seam records only as "every invocation", with no timestamps and no synchronisation primitive, so none of these is more supported by the spec than the others. Test 6 has the same problem for "crashed driver": the spec never says how a crash is induced.
suggestion: Pin the observable: state that the fake runner records a start and end timestamp per invocation (or a rendezvous the test controls), and phrase test 5 as "the recorded intervals of the round's role units overlap pairwise, and no non-role unit's interval overlaps any of them". For test 6, name the induced failure (e.g. the driver process is killed between spawn and the state update).

finding: Test 21 — "The plugin validates with `claude plugin validate`, and its hook payloads are asserted against fixtures" — is not a test a second engineer would reproduce. "Hook payloads" is ambiguous in both direction and identity: it could mean the JSON the client sends each hook, the JSON each hook emits back (the `SessionStart` additional context, the `PreToolUse` deny decision, the `Stop` block reason), or the declaration blocks in the plugin manifest. Which of the three hooks, and what a fixture pins (exact bytes, a subset of keys, exit code) is unstated. §6.2's own testable claim — that the `SessionStart` payload "is `tp resume --compact` and nothing else" — is never asserted anywhere.
suggestion: Split test 21 into named assertions: the manifest validates; the `SessionStart` hook's emitted additional context equals the output of `tp resume --compact` for the same state and carries nothing else; the `PreToolUse` hook emits a deny decision for each fenced path; the `Stop` hook emits a block reason naming the missing durable write. Say for each whether the fixture pins exact output or named keys.

finding: "Ids are unique within a run" is false for the ids §3.1 itself defines. A role unit's id is the role id, and a run executes the same role once per round, so `implementer` recurs in every review round; a record unit's id is the round number, which recurs across the review and audit phases; a retried `implement` unit reuses its task id. Anything an implementer builds on that uniqueness claim (a map keyed by id, a dedup of run.json rows, `last_failure` bookkeeping) breaks on the first multi-round run.
suggestion: Replace the claim with the true invariant — `(seq)` is unique within a run, `(kind, id)` is what `last_failure` matches on — and drop "unique within a run" or qualify it as "unique within an iteration".

finding: 'Ids are unique within a run' contradicts the id definitions in the same paragraph. A run spans multiple review/audit rounds, and a role unit's id is the role id, so `architect` recurs in every review round of the same run; an `implement` unit's task id can also recur after a reopen. Uniqueness within a run holds only for `$TP_UNIT_SEQ`. This matters because §4.2 clears `last_failure` on `(unit_kind, unit_id)` and because §6.3's allowlist is derived from the id.
suggestion: Weaken the claim to what is true — ids are unique within an iteration, `seq` is unique within a run — and re-check every consumer that relies on run-wide uniqueness (`last_failure` clearing, findings-file naming, escalation record naming) against the weaker guarantee.

finding: Round 2 added `TP_RUN_DIR` to the child environment and made it load-bearing in three other repaired sections — §5.2 builds `$TP_RUN_DIR/$TP_UNIT_SEQ-escalation.json` and makes its absence a usage error, §6.2 reads escalations from it, §6.3 makes it the switch that changes `tp review`/`tp audit`'s emitted findings path — but no section ever says what its value is. §3.5's log directory `.tp/runs/<run-id>/` is the obvious intent and is never equated to it.
suggestion: State the value where the variable is introduced: "`TP_RUN_DIR` is the run's artifact directory, `.tp/runs/<run-id>/` (§3.5); the driver creates it before spawning the first unit."

finding: The five child environment variables `TP_RUN_ID`, `TP_UNIT_ID`, `TP_UNIT_KIND`, `TP_UNIT_SEQ` and `TP_RUN_DIR` have no test, although three later sections are built on them: §5.2 derives the escalation path from `$TP_RUN_DIR/$TP_UNIT_SEQ`, §6.2 makes "`TP_UNIT_KIND` is set" the Stop hook's in-a-unit predicate, and §6.3 derives the findings path from `$TP_RUN_DIR/$TP_UNIT_SEQ-$TP_UNIT_ID`. Test 17 asserts only that a `runner.env` entry cannot override `TP_UNATTENDED`; nothing asserts these five are present, nor that the same override rule (§3.2: "the driver's own variables are applied after that merge") protects them too.
suggestion: Add a test that the fake runner records its own environment and asserts all five variables are set with the expected values for the unit (including `TP_UNIT_SEQ` matching the `run.json` row's `seq`), and extend test 17 to cover a `runner.env` attempt to override each of them, not just `TP_UNATTENDED`.

finding: The run lock at `.tp/locks/run-<base>.lock` drops the path hash the existing centralized lock carries (`.tp/locks/<base>-<hash>.lock`, REFERENCE.md), and that hash exists precisely because base names collide across directories. Two task files with the same base name under different directories — the exact case the existing scheme guards — would share one run lock, so a legitimate second `tp run` exits 4 with no explanation. The spec also does not say whether the run lock uses the same `lock_timeout_seconds` path or fails immediately.
suggestion: Use the existing naming (`run-<base>-<hash>.lock`, hashed from the resolved task-file path) or state that the run lock reuses `engine.LockFilePath`'s derivation with a `run-` prefix, and say that the run lock fails fast rather than waiting on `lock_timeout_seconds`.

finding: `TP_RUN_DIR` is listed among the five variables every child receives, and §3.3, §5.2 and §6.2/§6.3 all build paths from it, but the spec never states its value. §3.5 only says logs stream to `.tp/runs/<run-id>/…`, which implies `TP_RUN_DIR` = that directory, and the `*.ndjson` vs `.jsonl` extensions imply logs and findings share it — but neither is stated, nor whether the value is absolute or repo-relative. A hook or a child with a different working directory cannot resolve a relative value, and `tp escalate` (§5.2) keys its "outside a run" usage error on the variable's presence alone.
suggestion: Define `TP_RUN_DIR` explicitly as the absolute path of `.tp/runs/<run-id>`, state that the driver creates it before the first spawn, and say that logs and per-unit artifacts share it.

finding: §3.4 requires each unit to be attempted `1 + run_max_unit_retries` times, but §3.1's six-step loop has no retry step: step 4 spawns, step 5 re-reads state, step 6 checks caps and loops back to step 1, which re-derives units from the oracle. Nothing in the loop re-spawns a failed unit, and for a concurrent role iteration the spec never says whether a failed sibling is retried inside the same iteration (with successful siblings left alone) or whether the whole iteration repeats. §3.5's per-attempt `attempt` field also leaves it unclear whether a retry counts against `run_max_units`.
suggestion: Add the retry to §3.1's enumerated loop, state that a retry re-spawns only the failed unit within the same iteration, and say whether an attempt or a unit is what `run_max_units` and `totals.units` count.

finding: Round 2 added `{unit_kind}` to the `args` placeholder set, joining `{unit_id}` and `{log_path}` — but §3.1 already spawns every child with `TP_UNIT_KIND`, `TP_UNIT_ID`, `TP_UNIT_SEQ` and `TP_RUN_DIR`, from which the log path is derivable (§3.5's path is `<run-dir>/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl`). The only consumer the spec names for these three placeholders is the `TP_RUNNER` test seam, whose fake could read the same values from its environment. Each placeholder is surface an operator must learn, a doc row, and a new exit-2 failure mode (`A placeholder the driver cannot resolve is a usage error`), paying for nothing a real runner needs.
suggestion: Keep `{prompt}` and `{max_budget_usd}` (values a runner genuinely takes as arguments) and drop `{unit_id}`, `{unit_kind}` and `{log_path}` from the template vocabulary, letting the env contract of §3.1 be the single channel for unit identity; have the `TP_RUNNER` fake record `TP_UNIT_KIND`/`TP_UNIT_ID` from its environment. If a real runner does need one of them on the command line, name that runner in §3.2 so the placeholder is justified by a use rather than by a fixture.

finding: `TP_RUNNER` is described as both 'it outranks every other source of `runner`' and 'the env layer of the existing precedence, so no new precedence rule is introduced'. Those cannot both hold: §7 states the new fields resolve CLI > env > task override > project config > built-in, so a CLI-supplied runner would outrank the env layer. Either a CLI source for `runner` exists and the 'outranks every other source' claim is false, or the seam really is a new top-of-precedence rule the sentence denies.
suggestion: Pick one: state that `TP_RUNNER` sits at the env layer and is therefore overridden by an explicit CLI runner flag, or state that it is a test-only override above CLI and acknowledge it as a deliberate exception to §7's precedence.

finding: The new durable-write column gives `decompose` the predicate "The task file holds at least one task". That is satisfiable before the unit starts — after a partial import, on a retry (attempt 2 of `1 + run_max_unit_retries`, §3.4), or on any cycle whose shell already holds tasks — so §6.2's Stop hook lets the unit end and §3.3's "the driver's own success test" passes for a unit that imported nothing. A predicate meant to prove work happened must be a change, and this one is a state.
suggestion: Make it a change: "The task file's task count increased" (with the pre-unit count supplied as the unit's baseline, per the §6.2 finding), or key it on the import's own record rather than on the file's contents.

finding: Two cells of the new Durable-write column are relative, not observable: `review-resolve` is `The spec's hash changed` and `audit-fix` is `HEAD advanced`. Both require a pre-unit baseline, and §6.2 states the Stop hook's predicates `are observable, not inferences` and that it `never reads .tp/run.json`. Nothing in §3.5 stores a per-unit baseline hash or start SHA, so honouring these two rows forces a new stored artifact (or a git call inside a 10s-timeout hook) that the spec has not budgeted — new surface introduced by a table cell rather than by a decision.
suggestion: Either name the baseline as part of the child's environment (e.g. a `TP_UNIT_BASELINE` the driver computes once per unit, so the hook compares without new files), or restate both predicates as absolute conditions already on disk — for `review-resolve`, that the round's findings carry a resolution status; for `audit-fix`, that the finding's row is marked addressed. Whatever is chosen, §3.3's fourth column and §6.2 must name the same observable, since the spec says both read the same condition.

finding: "`SIGINT` and `SIGTERM` set `interrupted` on the same terms: in-flight children finish" is not achievable with a default spawn. A Ctrl-C at the terminal delivers `SIGINT` to the entire foreground process group, so the children receive it too and die with the driver; the guarantee only holds if the driver puts each child in its own process group (`Setpgid`) — and then the operator's second Ctrl-C has no way to stop them either. The spec asserts the outcome without naming the mechanism or the escape hatch.
suggestion: State that children are spawned in their own process group so a terminal signal reaches only the driver, and say what a second signal does (e.g. same behaviour, or a documented force path that kills children and still writes run state).

finding: Retry semantics are defined only for a lone unit. For a parallel `review-role`/`audit-role` batch the spec does not say whether the driver waits for all siblings before retrying the failed one, retries it alongside the still-running siblings, or respawns the whole batch; nor whether a sibling's failure aborts the iteration. It also never says whether an attempt counts toward `run_max_units` (§3.5's row model — one appended row per spawn with an `attempt` field — suggests yes, but `cap-units` says "Executed units", which reads as distinct units), so two implementations can differ by a factor of `1 + run_max_unit_retries` on the same cap.
suggestion: State the retry policy for a concurrent batch (wait for all siblings, then retry only failed units, batch unchanged) and state explicitly whether a retry attempt increments the `run_max_units` counter.

finding: Two of §3.4's stop behaviours are untested. (a) `interrupted`: "`SIGINT` and `SIGTERM` set `interrupted` on the same terms: in-flight children finish, no new unit is spawned, and the run state is written before the driver exits" — no test in 10.1-10.5 sends a signal, and test 3's "Each cap produces its own `stop_reason`" does not reach it, since `interrupted` is not a cap. (b) The overshoot rule: "Caps are evaluated between iterations only... a run can overshoot its wall-clock and budget caps by at most one iteration; the driver kills nothing." This is the claim most likely to be implemented as an eager kill, it is directly observable with the fake runner (a long unit spawned just under the cap must still be allowed to exit), and nothing asserts it.
suggestion: Add two §10.1 tests: a `SIGTERM` delivered mid-iteration lets the in-flight child exit, spawns no further unit, and leaves `.tp/run.json` with `stop_reason: interrupted` and the child's row updated; and a unit spawned while under the wall-clock cap runs to completion after the cap elapses, with the run stopping at the following cap check and no child killed.

finding: `TP_RUN_DIR` is dereferenced by four sections — the findings path (§3.3, §6.3), the escalation record (§5.2), the Stop hook predicate (§6.2) — but no section ever binds it to a value. §3.5 defines the log path as `.tp/runs/<run-id>/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl` without saying that `TP_RUN_DIR` is `.tp/runs/<run-id>/`, so the identity every consumer assumes is inferred rather than stated, and whether it is absolute or repo-relative (which decides whether an agent's write allowlist can match it) is undecided.
suggestion: Define `TP_RUN_DIR` once in §3.5 — the absolute path to `.tp/runs/<run-id>/`, created before the first unit of the run is spawned — and have §3.3/§5.2/§6.2/§6.3 refer to that definition.

finding: Three testable claims about the oracle's new surface have no test. (a) "a non-concurrent kind is never returned alongside another unit" — test 5 tests the driver's spawning, not what `next_units` may contain, and this is an invariant of `tp resume --json` that is cheap to assert directly over fixture states. (b) "`next_action`'s `command`, `brief_command` and `payload` render `next_units[0]` when the array is non-empty" — the mirroring rule between the human surface and the machine surface is exactly the kind of pair that drifts, and nothing pins it. (c) The two `no-units` cases are distinguished in prose ("a phase whose work is blocked, and a phase awaiting an operator decision") with "`next_action.summary` names what the phase is waiting for", but no test asserts either case produces `no-units` with a non-empty summary.
suggestion: Add a §10.1 or §10.2 test over fixture cycle states: for every phase, `next_units` is either a single non-concurrent unit or a set of concurrent role units of one kind; `next_action.command`/`brief_command`/`payload` equal `next_units[0]`'s when the array is non-empty; and each of the two blocked cases yields `[]`, `stop_reason: no-units` and a `next_action.summary` naming the wait.

finding: §4.2 gives `last_failure` two write triggers — "When a unit exits non-zero, **or closes with a failed quality gate**" — and a content contract for `summary`: "tp-authored — the failing command and the gate's own output when a gate failed — never the child's prose". Test 20 covers only the non-zero-exit trigger and asserts nothing about `summary`. The gate branch is the one that matters, because it is the branch where a plausible implementation reaches for the child's output, and the whole point of the field (§4.2: "never the child's prose", Non-Goal 6) is that it must not. The object's field set `{unit_kind, unit_id, phase, exit_code, summary, at}` is also unasserted.
suggestion: Extend test 20: a unit whose `tp done` fails the quality gate writes `last_failure` carrying the gate's own output and the failing command, and a unit whose child printed a plausible failure narrative does not have any of that prose in `summary`; assert the exact key set of the written object.

finding: §4.2 says "tp records a `last_failure` object" for two different events with two different writers and never separates them. A non-zero unit exit is observed by the driver; a close with a failed quality gate happens inside the child's own `tp done`. The child path leaves three of the six fields underivable outside a run — `unit_kind`, `unit_id` and `phase` come from `TP_UNIT_*`, which are unset when a developer runs `tp done` interactively — and the spec does not say whether `tp done` writes `last_failure` at all in that case, nor what it writes for those fields.
suggestion: State the writer per event: the driver writes it on a non-zero child exit from the unit row it already holds; `tp done` writes it on a gate failure only when `TP_UNIT_KIND` is set, and does not write one outside a run.

finding: The unattended fence covers the three CLAUDE.md decisions but not the run caps this version introduces. §6.2 deliberately leaves shell invocations outside the PreToolUse matcher, so an unattended child can run `tp set --workflow run_max_units=…` (or `run_max_wall_clock_seconds`, `run_max_budget_usd`, `run_max_unit_retries`) through a supported route; since §7 resolves at read time and §3.4 evaluates caps between iterations, that raises the very backstop §3.4 calls the last defence. This is structurally the forged-approval pattern §5.1 exists to close, one field set later.
suggestion: Extend the §5.1 table to reject raising any resolved `run_*` cap under `TP_UNATTENDED`, with the same equal-or-lower allowance, or state explicitly that the driver snapshots caps at run start and never re-reads them — and say which.

finding: §5.1 defines mode activation with three conditions — "present, non-empty and not `0`" — but test 16 exercises only `TP_UNATTENDED=1` and the variable's absence. The two discriminating cases, `TP_UNATTENDED=` (present but empty) and `TP_UNATTENDED=0`, are exactly where two engineers would write contradictory tests, and they are the values a wrapper script is most likely to produce accidentally. Other truthy-looking values (`false`, `no`, `00`) are also unspecified: the rule as written makes `TP_UNATTENDED=false` active, which is surprising enough to deserve an explicit assertion.
suggestion: Extend test 16 to a value table: `1` and any other non-empty non-`0` string (e.g. `false`) activate the mode; `0`, the empty string and an unset variable do not. State in §5.1 that the comparison is against the literal string `0` only, so the `false` case is a deliberate result rather than an oversight.

finding: §5.2 makes `tp escalate` the supported route out of a user-only decision, but §5.1's table still describes the three refusals only as `Exit 2, hint naming it a user-approved decision`. A unit that hits the fence therefore learns what it may not do but not what it should do instead, so the escalation route has to be carried in the driver's `{prompt}` or discovered by the model — a wasted attempt (and, under §3.4, a consumed retry) each time it is not.
suggestion: State in §5.1 that each refusal's hint names the exact escalation invocation for that decision (`tp escalate --decision skip-gate|raise-review-cap|raise-audit-cap|import-force --evidence ...`), and extend test 16 to assert the hint carries it. That makes the `decision` enum load-bearing — it is the value the refusal hands the unit — instead of a vocabulary the unit must map onto by itself.

finding: The round-2 rewrite dropped the sentence "The unit is the writer; a tp command that refuses under §5.1 prints the hint and the unit records the escalation from it." Nothing replaced the link: §5.1's table still describes only "Exit 2, hint naming it a user-approved decision", and §5.2's new `tp escalate` is never connected to those three refusals. The one path an unattended unit is expected to take after a fail-closed refusal is now unstated in both sections, and §5.1's three hints do not name the command that exists to handle them.
suggestion: Restore the link in one place: add to §5.1 that each refusal hint names `tp escalate --decision <skip-gate|raise-review-cap|raise-audit-cap|import-force>` as the supported next step, and state in §5.2 that the unit — not tp itself — runs it.

finding: §5.2 goes out of its way to say `notify_cmd` "is invoked on every non-converged stop, not on escalation alone", and then pins four further properties: exec'd without a shell, split on whitespace, with `TP_STOP_REASON`, `TP_RUN_ID` and (on escalation) `TP_ESCALATION_PATH` in its environment, and an exit code that "is reported and changes nothing". Test 18 exercises exactly the one case the prose warns is not the whole rule — invocation on escalation. Nothing tests invocation on `cap-units`/`unit-failure`/`no-units`/`interrupted`, non-invocation on `converged`, the environment contract, the no-shell splitting (a `notify_cmd` containing a shell metacharacter must not be interpreted), or that a failing `notify_cmd` leaves `stop_reason` untouched.
suggestion: Add a §10.3 test: `notify_cmd` fires once per non-converged stop reason and not on `converged`; it receives `TP_STOP_REASON`/`TP_RUN_ID` (plus `TP_ESCALATION_PATH` only on escalation); a value containing `;` or `&&` is passed as literal argv words; and a `notify_cmd` exiting non-zero leaves the recorded `stop_reason` and exit code of `tp run` unchanged.

finding: The plugin preflight has a precise, testable contract and no test: "if `tp` is absent from `PATH` or older than `0.35.0`, it fails with the install command rather than degrading quietly. The minimum is `plugin.json`'s own version, compared against `tp --version`." §10.4's four tests cover manifest validation, the deny matcher, the Stop hook and the run-scoped findings path — none touches preflight. The comparison rule also leaves a boundary open: is a `tp --version` exactly equal to `plugin.json`'s version accepted ("older than" says yes), and how does a pre-release or dev-build version string compare?
suggestion: Add a §10.4 test: preflight passes on an equal version, passes on a higher one, fails with the install command on a lower one and on `tp` absent from `PATH`. State in §6.1 how a non-release version string (e.g. a dev build) is compared, so the test has a defined expectation.

finding: The preflight has no host. §6.1 requires the plugin to fail with an install command when `tp` is absent from `PATH` or older than `plugin.json`'s version, but §6.2's hook table declares only three events (`SessionStart`, `PreToolUse`, `Stop`) and none of them performs a version check, and §10.4's plugin tests do not cover it. The implementer must guess which event runs the check, what "fails" means for that event (blocking output, non-zero exit, injected context), and how `tp --version`'s string is compared to a semver minimum when `tp` is absent (the command itself fails).
suggestion: Name the event that runs the preflight (most plausibly `SessionStart`, before the orientation injection), define the failure behaviour in that event's terms, and specify the comparison (semver compare of `tp --version` output against `plugin.json`'s version; a missing binary is the same failure).

finding: §7 exempts `notify_cmd` from the layered path ('read from `.tp/local.json` only') and in the next paragraph says `tp config --resolved`, `tp config --extract` and `tp validate --project` cover the new fields 'on the same terms as every existing workflow field'. `--extract` writes workflow values into the committed `.tp/config.json`, which is precisely the file `notify_cmd` is never read from, so extracting it produces a value that silently does nothing — the same drift class §3.5 argues against for run state.
suggestion: State the exemption on all three surfaces: `--extract` must skip `notify_cmd`, `validate --project` must flag it as misplaced when it appears in `.tp/config.json`, and `--resolved` should show its source as `.tp/local.json`.

finding: `location_clusters` is added to `tp review --merge` and `tp review --status`, is explicitly `reporting only`, and §4.1 fixes `next_units` as `the only field the driver parses` — so the new key lands in exactly the two payloads the unattended driver and the review-record unit read, and in neither of the two the human reads (`tp run --status` in §3.5 carries `spec_coverage_clean_rounds`, `role_streaks` and `divergence`, not clusters). Its stated motive is that an unattended driver misreads duplicate counts, yet no component that stops or continues a run consumes it. §7's `--compact` rule covers run state only, so nothing strips these bytes from review output either.
suggestion: Either route `location_clusters` where its reader is — add it to §3.5's `tp run --status` on a review-phase stop, next to the divergence signals — or state explicitly which agent-facing decision consumes it in `--merge`. Also give it a `--compact` disposition in §7 (stripped, like per-unit rows), so the round-per-round cost of the extra array is bounded.

finding: §8a's arity paragraph says every command's `Args` validator exits 2, "matching §9's definition of a usage error". §9 is the Non-Goals list (seven numbered items) and contains no definition of a usage error — nor does any word of it mention exit codes. The only place the spec defines the term is §3.2 ("A placeholder the driver cannot resolve is a usage error (exit 2)"), with §5.2 using it again for `tp escalate` outside a run. A tester writing test 28 has no cited definition to check the new behaviour against.
suggestion: Point the reference at §3.2 (or state the definition inline: a usage error is a malformed invocation, exits 2, and is raised before any effect), and keep §9 out of it.

finding: Test 25 asserts only the positive clustering case ("a location reported by two roles under different classes"). §8a defines the entry as "one entry per `location` carrying findings from more than one role, `{location, roles[], severities[], count}`", which makes the negative case the discriminating one: a location that one role reported twice under two classes must NOT produce a cluster. Without it, an implementation that clusters on `location` alone passes test 25. The entry's field set and the meaning of `count` (findings at that location, or distinct roles?) are also unasserted, and `severities[]` is not stated to be deduplicated or ordered — two engineers would write different expected values.
suggestion: Extend test 25 with the same-role-twice case producing no cluster, and pin one full expected entry (including whether `roles[]`/`severities[]` are sorted and deduplicated, and what `count` counts).

finding: Of the five child environment variables added in round 2, `TP_RUN_ID` has no consumer inside a unit anywhere in the spec: every child-written artifact is addressed through `TP_RUN_DIR` plus `TP_UNIT_SEQ`/`TP_UNIT_ID` (§3.3, §5.2, §6.2, §6.3), and the run id reaches the only component that needs it — `notify_cmd` — through `TP_STOP_REASON`/`TP_RUN_ID` in §5.2's separate notify environment. An env var is a documented contract the plugin's hooks, the agent definitions and SKILL.md must all carry, so an unused one is pure surface.
suggestion: Drop `TP_RUN_ID` from the child environment (§3.1) unless a unit-side use is named — the run directory already identifies the run — or name that use in the same sentence, e.g. if a unit is expected to write it into a commit trailer or an escalation record.

finding: `Ids are unique within a run` does not hold for the id definitions the same paragraph gives: a run spans multiple review and audit rounds, so a `review-role` unit's role id (and an `audit-fix` unit's finding index) recurs every round. The spec's own paths are already seq-prefixed for exactly that reason (`$TP_RUN_DIR/$TP_UNIT_SEQ-$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson`, `$TP_UNIT_SEQ-escalation.json`), so the sentence promises a property nothing relies on while inviting a reader to think `TP_UNIT_SEQ` is redundant.
suggestion: Replace the sentence with what is true and load-bearing: ids are unique within an iteration, `seq` is the run-unique key, and `last_failure` matches on `(unit_kind, unit_id)` deliberately so a later round's success of the same role clears the earlier round's failure.

finding: The spec introduces the general `spend_key` mechanism and then keeps a hardcoded special case beside it: `the driver reads one number from the final line of that unit's log: total_cost_usd for claude, spend_key for any runner that declares one`. The `claude` template is itself configuration, so it can declare `spend_key: "total_cost_usd"` and be read by the same path — the special case buys nothing and costs a branch in the driver, a sentence in the docs, and a second thing a reader must hold to predict spend behaviour.
suggestion: Rewrite §3.2's Spend paragraph as one rule — the driver reads `spend_key` from the final log line, and reports `spend: null` when the resolved runner declares none — and add `spend_key: "total_cost_usd"` to the `claude` built-in's definition (the `opencode` built-in already declares none, which is the same rule with the opposite outcome).

finding: Two runner-resolution rules with explicit failure modes have no test. "`runner` ... takes one of three shapes: a built-in template name, a runner object, or a map from unit kind to either of those with a `default` key covering the rest. A map missing `default` is a usage error" — test 10 covers placeholder resolution only, so neither the per-kind map (the feature §3.2 spends a paragraph justifying) nor the missing-`default` usage error is exercised, and it is unstated whether the error is raised at resolution time or only when an uncovered kind is reached. Separately, "Every child is spawned with stdin closed" — named as "the hardest unattended failure to diagnose" — is directly observable (the fake runner reads stdin and must see EOF) and untested.
suggestion: Add to §10.2: a per-kind map routes `audit-role` to one `cmd` and every other kind to `default`; a map without `default` exits 2 before any child is spawned; and the fake runner records that its stdin is at EOF.

finding: `{max_budget_usd}` is listed as a general placeholder available to any `runner.args`, but its zero-value behaviour is defined only for the built-in `claude` template ("omits the budget flag entirely"). For a custom runner whose `args` embed `{max_budget_usd}` and a resolved `run_max_unit_budget_usd` of 0, the spec supports three readings — substitute the literal `0`, drop just that argument, or raise the exit-2 usage error for "a placeholder the driver cannot resolve" — and each produces a different child command line.
suggestion: State the rule once for all runners: a 0 budget removes the argument containing `{max_budget_usd}` (and an immediately preceding flag argument, if the template pairs them), or make the built-in behaviour a template property rather than a placeholder rule.

finding: The new row-timing paragraph justifies atomic writes as "because concurrent siblings write rows in the same iteration". The siblings are child processes, and §3.1 step 4 plus §3.5's "observability, not truth" make the driver the sole writer of `.tp/run.json` — no child writes a row. The real reason for temp+rename is that `tp run --status` (and a crash) can observe the file mid-write.
suggestion: Replace the rationale with the true one: "Both writes are atomic (temp + rename) because `tp run --status` may read the file at any moment and a crashed driver must not leave a truncated one."

finding: Three assertions about `.tp/run.json` are stated as load-bearing and left untested. "That file is observability, not truth: no decision — the driver's or a hook's — reads it back" is testable as an absence (a run with the file deleted or corrupted mid-run behaves identically), and §6.2 repeats the hook half ("It never reads `.tp/run.json`"). "The accrued totals therefore restart at zero on a new run" is a one-line assertion nothing makes. And "Both writes are atomic (temp + rename), because concurrent siblings write rows in the same iteration" is the concurrency hazard of the whole design, yet test 12 checks only the single-unit before/after shape.
suggestion: Add to §10.2: a run whose `.tp/run.json` is deleted after the first iteration completes normally and produces the same stop reason; a second run over a cycle with a prior run's totals starts its totals at zero; and a round of N concurrent role units yields exactly N rows with no lost update.

finding: "When `TP_RUN_DIR` is set, `tp review` and `tp audit` emit that same path as the role's output file" — but the path in the same sentence is `$TP_RUN_DIR/$TP_UNIT_SEQ-$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson`, so TP_RUN_DIR alone is not enough to build it. The condition and the template disagree about which variables must be present, leaving the behaviour undefined when TP_RUN_DIR is set and TP_UNIT_SEQ or TP_UNIT_ID is not (which is exactly what a hand-run `tp review` inside a run's shell would produce).
suggestion: Condition on the full set: "When `TP_RUN_DIR`, `TP_UNIT_SEQ` and `TP_UNIT_ID` are all set … otherwise the emitted filename is unchanged."

finding: §6.4 requires that "Every hook the plugin ships declares a `timeout` of 10 seconds and exits non-zero rather than hanging", and names it "the one failure mode in this design that the driver cannot observe from outside" — that is, the only defence is the declaration itself. No test asserts it, though it is a trivial manifest assertion, and §10.4's test 21 ("validates with `claude plugin validate`") does not imply it: a missing or larger `timeout` is valid to the validator.
suggestion: Add to test 21 (or a new §10.4 item): every hook entry in the shipped plugin manifest declares `timeout: 10`, asserted by enumerating the hooks rather than spot-checking one.

finding: The workflow-field table gives `runner`'s range as 'Built-in name or object', while §3.2 defines three accepted shapes, the third being a map from unit kind to a name or object with a required `default` key. A reader validating config against the §7 table would reject the per-kind map that §3.2 calls the point of the feature.
suggestion: Change the range cell to 'Built-in name, runner object, or per-kind map with `default` (§3.2)'.
